segments.text: Can I go? Moramse. Salaam alaikum. Jumbo.

Distinguished panelists who are coming on board, colleagues, partners, welcome to this plenary on aligning pre-service midwifery education with international and national standards. Today, we are thinking through the African midwifery acceleration, educate, deploy, and retain. Across our continent, midwives are critical to reducing preventable maternal and newborn deaths.

Yet, the quality of care depends on the education they receive, the competencies they acquire, and health systems in which they practice and how supportive those health systems are. We must move beyond the curriculum, the documents, to nationally recognized, adequately resourced, and contextualized that produce competent graduates. We will hear from the International Confederation of Midwives on international competencies and from the United Nations UNFPA on the updated sample curricula.

We will also hear how Rwanda has integrated the national curriculum and harmonized it to the international standards. Further, we will also hear from ESCOCOM on regional, educational, and regulatory practical implementation pathways that are measurable within our context. Without further ado, I want to invite our panelists.

First, we will have presentations from ICM and UNFPA. I will invite Dr. Kate Stringer, our ICM midwifery expert, educator, and multi-professional faculty development expert. Please welcome her, the African way.
That is not the African way. Ah, look, look, look, look, look, look, look. Thank you.
Let me check if my, oh, that's something. Okay, no worries. Okay, you're good.
Thank you. Good morning, all. Thank you for having us here today for us to speak on one of my own personal favorite topics and also a critical topic for ICM.

Before I do the main body of my talk, I just want to reflect on where we're at with the 2019 WHO Strengthening Quality Midwifery Education Framework. We've come a long way since 2019. Many, many more midwives are in practice and providing care for women and girls.

And we have also many more midwives in leadership positions. But we still know that many midwives are not the leads of pre-service midwifery education programs. And in many settings, midwives are not necessarily the educators of future midwives.

We also heard yesterday that there's still significant fragmentation or lack of alignment between midwifery programs across the region and also in regulation and scope of practice. So I'm really pleased to see that a regulatory body was one of the priorities this morning. So these are the essential competencies for midwifery practice, and they were updated in 2024.

And these competencies outline the minimum knowledge, skills, and behaviors that all midwives should have. And only when midwives are educated to all of these essential competencies will they be able to provide 90% of sexual and reproductive health care and have the significant impact that we know midwives can have. In 2024, we added a new category, Category 2, which rightly demonstrates the midwife's critical role in sexual and reproductive health and rights.

The competencies are not necessarily new in this category, but we brought them together to really demonstrate the midwife's role in this area. And ICM has recently been undertaking curricular reviews in five countries in Africa and Asia with midwives associations and other partners. And we found these competencies are often underrepresented in curricula or that there's an overemphasis on theory-based content.

And where midwifery practice placements are already in existence, students may not have the specific opportunities to practice family planning competencies, provide contraception, and demonstrate what they know and learn in all of the different midwifery contexts, including community-based care. ICM has a mission and vision that all women all over the world have the same quality of care. And that relies on all students and midwives having the same quality of pre-service midwifery education.

So I just put this slide in there as a reminder. I've been working with French colleagues in Francophone Africa recently. And all of the ICM's resources, tools, guides, and standards are also available on our website in French and in Spanish.

So if that is your preferred language, please go to the website and you're able to download those things also in French. So the ICM essential competencies are for all midwives, regardless of your educational pathway. And as I was preparing for this session, I was reflecting on conversations that I hear all over Africa and also all over the world.

What is a direct entry midwife? What is a post-nursing midwife? What does that mean? And I reflected on what do women and families want? When I had my babies 20 years ago, I didn't know what type of midwife I had. And I didn't need to know. What I wanted to know was that she was safe, that she was kind, she was knowledgeable, and she knew what to do in an emergency.

And I think that all mothers in this room probably are exactly the same. Women want safe, competent midwives that provide rights-affirming care. And the only way that we achieve that is that all midwives have the same set of competencies, and that is assessed with the same exit point.

So ICM also has global standards for midwifery education programs, and they set out the minimum time requirement of these programs. And the essential competencies and the time requirement of the programs is based on global evidence and WHO standards and guidelines. And the programs must have a minimum of 40% theory and a minimum of 50% practice.

Midwifery is an applied practice, and midwives and students must have the opportunity to develop those experiences in practice. And those practice experiences must cover the full scope of midwifery practice. So that includes community care, public health care settings, and tertiary referral settings.

Regardless of your entry point into midwifery education, we all need to graduate as midwives. There's no hierarchy in midwives, and we need all of the different pathways. But global evidence suggests that direct entry pathways are often more cost-efficient.

Midwives graduate feeling more confident to practice across the full scope of practice. And also, they support retention because the investment in pre-service midwifery education stays in maternal and newborn health pathway. Sometimes when people have dual registration, nurses are expected to go into other areas, and that significant investment in educating midwives does not stay in maternal and newborn health.

So ICM and other partners have been working to provide additional resources and tools throughout the last five and six or ten years. And we have the global standards for midwifery education, and these standards set out the minimum core requirements to enable national systems to have quality pre-service midwifery education programmes. They're designed to be used as benchmarks.

They can be contextualised, but you can use them in your setting to review your own programmes and identify what areas may need strengthening. Last year, we launched the global standards for midwife faculty development. And as an educator myself, I feel really strongly about faculty development.

If I'm not confident in a particular skill or competency myself, I'm very reluctant or unable to be able to teach that in a quality way that students need and deserve. So ongoing faculty development is a critical step to quality education. And sometimes the area that is under-invested or under-recognised.

These standards set out the key elements that you should be looking at when you're developing faculty development programmes. And faculty development needs to be an ongoing development process. New evidence and guidance exists all the time in midwifery, and therefore to maintain the quality, we need to continually review our programmes and also faculty's skills and competencies.

And then the other area that I really feel is under-invested or maybe under-recognised is midwifery regulation. Midwifery regulation is critical to ensure that the scope of practice is aligned to what is happening in pre-service midwifery education programmes. It's a waste of resources if midwives are supported in pre-service midwifery programmes to develop all of the essential competencies, but when they arrive in practice, they're not enabled and supported to be able to deliver the care that they have been educated to do.

In addition, regulation needs to oversee the quality assurance of midwifery education programmes. And that needs to happen in public or private settings. What we sometimes hear is that in government education programmes, there's ongoing curricular view and investment, but perhaps the oversight isn't as strong in private settings or in private hospitals.

And we need to ensure that the same quality of pre-service education happens in all settings. My colleague is going to talk about the sample curricula, which we hope will be a really significant support for all of you. So I won't spend too long there.

And then just to conclude, we need to move beyond just curricular changes. In fact, sometimes making curricular changes is one of the easiest steps to improving quality pre-service midwifery education. We need to make sure that there is one standardised exit point for all midwifery programmes.

There's ongoing investment in midwife faculty, and that's not in standalone programmes, but they continue all of the time. We need to work towards aligned national and regional midwifery programmes so that all midwives and women, whichever country they are in in Africa, know that they can receive the same quality of care. And strong and effective regulatory systems, so scope of practice is aligned and it meets the essential competencies.
There's quality assurance of midwifery education, and there's ongoing assessment of competency through CPD and relicensing programmes. Thank you. Thank you very much, Kate.

I hope we are all ready to integrate the ICM competencies within our programmes. And I think the idea is that the International Confederation of Midwives comes up with this evidence-based structures but it is up to us to contextualise them and implement them. Thank you.
Our next speaker is Dr. Duncan Shikoku. He's the UNFPA Headquarters Technical Specialist in Midwifery. Let us welcome him with a round of applause.
Good morning, everyone. I can't hear you well. This is African people in Africa, always very energetic.
Good morning. Good morning. Thank you so much.

Yeah, so before I start, I know we are all here because of the midwives and we all understand why we need to invest in midwives. And some of us from the settings where we've come from, we've come a long way when it comes to midwifery and with a lot of resistance in some of the countries. And testament to this day, you've really invested a lot in this and we continue to appreciate the key progress that you are making and also the partnerships you are making with all the government partners to ensure that we are investing in midwives so that at the centre of our maternity units, we only have midwives providing the care that we need.

And some arguments are that in some countries, some people still believe that you don't need a midwife. Anyone else, anyone can provide the needed support to women in labour and childbirth, but we all know that when this happens, we also have catastrophic effects within our maternity departments. And this reminds me of what our West African brothers usually teach us, that you don't, normally you don't take a goat for hunting simply because you don't have a dog.

You don't take a goat for hunting simply because you don't have a dog. We have to invest in the best dogs and these are the midwives. Let's not pretend that we can replace midwives with other existing cadres in maternity units.

Let's put our hands together and invest in midwives. And as we plan to invest more in midwives, when we look at the current evidence globally around the education of midwives, there are also challenges. And some of these challenges, as we know, contributing to the substandard training of midwives include the curricula.

And not just the curricula, but also the faculty that we expect to deliver this curricula are inadequately prepared and the institutions are also not prepared to teach the students to the best of the competencies as we expect. And largely most of the teaching methodologies are largely theoretical and we expect that as a midwife, you are a competent person who is hands-on and skills training is key to your performance. And so this WHO seven-step approach has already been highlighted by Kate is a key driving factor for us when it comes to investments in midwifery and it highlights the key steps that we need to strengthen, particularly for us to be able to have competent midwives graduating from the schools so that they can be able to provide the quality of the care that we deserve.

As already mentioned, UNFPA and ICM over the last couple of years with the contribution of majority of you in the room have contributed in the development of the global sample curriculum. And we have the sample curricula both for direct entry midwives as well as the post-nursing midwives. And we believe that these are flexible entry routes for our countries for us to be able to train these midwives.

And good to note is that these curricula have been aligned to the latest ICM essential competencies for midwifery practice and they are meant for us to contextualize within our national setups. We need to adapt these to our local needs at the country level. And throughout the curriculum, the two curriculum we've provided adequate hours to ensure that there is space for our midwifery faculty to adopt and ensure that some of the needs they have that may not be captured within this curricula are well embedded at the national level.

And key to note here is that there's a strong emphasis around clinical training and the practice sections. As you look at the distribution of the hours within the curricula, we expected that at least over half of the hours are dedicated to clinical practice for the midwife so that as they come out, then we expect clinically fit people who are able to practice within the settings with limited support. And just a high level overview about the sample curriculum, we have the section one which really provides an overview or rather program guidance on how countries can be able to review their curriculum and also adapt this curricula to their existing needs.

So it will give you a guidance on how you can develop the curriculum or review the existing programs within your country and also highlight some of the learning outcomes, the key attributes we expect from the faculty who are teaching these midwifery students and also what we expect the students who are coming out of these programs to look like. And we expect that by the end of this training, we don't want to have students who just know who are good at memorizing stuff. We want to, by the end of the training program, we want to have students who both know what they are doing but can also do what they are expected to do in terms of clinical skills and therefore even integrating the clinical assessments within their training so that as we review and assess the students in terms of their theory competencies, then we are also able to ensure that by the time of graduation, the students are practically fit, equipped with the necessary skills and competencies for them to practice independently within the maternity units.

As you can look at the two curricula here, this is just a demonstration of how the hours have been allocated. So if you look at the direct entry program, this one has about 4,600 hours compared to the post-nursing curriculum which has about 1,000 hours less compared to the direct entry curriculum. But key to note is that for the two curricula, the distribution of the number of hours when it comes to the clinical practice is the same.

We expect that at least 50% of the hours will be spent in clinical practice with at least 10% being left for the simulation learning for the students so that they can safely practice within the learning environments before they go out to the clinical setups and with 40% expected for them to be able to learn the theory that we need. And as earlier highlighted, we have about 140 hours here left for the countries to include any other components they feel are not captured within the curriculum and also dedicate about 140 hours for the students just to also allow them to learn on their own through the self-directed learning. And this just highlights one of the curricula, the direct entry curricula, the distribution of the content across the years, all totaling to the 4,600.

And just a modern structure, we expect that from this curricula, we are mapping the student expected learning outcomes to the teaching methodologies that will enable these students to acquire these competencies and also integrated with the right assessment procedures so that we are not only having theoretical experts but also competent experts in the practical setups. Now, to help us also understand what is happening within the countries, the UNFPA through our midwifery network, which is a network mapping out the midwifery expertise within the countries that we support, we also wanted to know what is happening around midwifery education, particularly when it comes to curriculum and faculty development. And it will be interesting for you to note that direct entry programs are still the leading when it comes to the key program, the predominant national programs at the country level with at least 60% of these programs being the direct entry programs, both at the diploma level and also at the bachelor's level.

And if we look at an assessment when if these countries have any room for carrying out curricular reviews in the next year or so, it's also encouraging to note that at least half of the countries have at least planned to have their reviews for 2077. And also very encouraging that some of them have already confirmed and budgeted these in their national budgets and for their remaining countries, discussions are still ongoing and we hope that as some of you are still here, we expect that by the end of this forum, you will definitely go and have these budgets within your national budgets to have the review of the curricula. And a very key component that we are looking at here when it comes to the training and education of midwives is the simulation component to ensure that we are not overloading our students with the theory but we are empowering them with opportunities to learn the skills within the training institutions.

But if you look at what is happening within majority of our countries, over about 60% of our countries have no policy or standards when it comes to simulation in midwifery education, clearly highlighting a gap that we need to invest in around simulation education because we expect by the time the students are going to the clinical areas, they have at least an idea of what they expected and this can only be through the simulation exposure that we hope our students can get through our institutions. And just as I finish, we also wanted to see what do countries consider as priorities for them when it comes to support around curricular review process. It is here that we note that majority of the countries feel support around capacity building for the educators is one of the key top priority for them and this clearly highlights what I had mentioned earlier that reviewing a curriculum is just one component of the process but the person who is going to teach this curriculum needs to be strengthened with the necessary capacity so that they can be able to deliver these competencies.

And as I finish, just to note that it is an essential component for us to ensure that we have strong faculty development programs within our units and we carried these studies within Kenya starting from the review of the curriculum and also getting experiences from the teachers as well as the students because there can be no discussion about the students without their participation and so we also got some experiences from the students and what they feel. And clearly from here, students feel like for us to have a responsive curriculum, they need to have educated faculty, they need to have adequate clinical sites for them to achieve the necessary case loads and also to be educated as competent students and graduate midwives. Thank you so much.
Wow, wow. Let us give him a round of applause. You know, what I love is that as an educator, when we are told to develop a curriculum, we used to beat about the bush like crazy.

Anybody in the house who can read me? And now we have a full curriculum, a sample curriculum that we don't have to crack our heads about it, just implement. Thank you very much. Thank you for that presentation.
I want to welcome on the stage Dr. Jillian Main. Dr. Jillian Main is our newly appointed president of East Central Southern African College of Nursing and Midwifery. Welcome.

Our next panelist is our new Dr. Olive Tenge. She is now a full chief midwife, an example that Rwanda is running faster than the rest of us, and that she is a midwife officer in the Ministry of Health. Welcome.
I'll keep my flag down. Thank you, colleagues. And before we continue, I just want to ask one question from our bosses, the ICM.

Kate, as countries revise their direct entry and post-nursing curricula, what evidence should education institutions and regulators require to demonstrate that graduates have achieved the essential competencies for safe, independent, and effective midwifery practice? Over to you. Thank you, Doreen. Having a robust curricula on paper is only a very small part of the step.

To make sure graduates have the competencies, there needs to be really effective assessment prior to graduation so that usually needs to cover theory and then also practical exams. It's really helpful if there's kind of a standardized clinical logbook or record of students' clinical experiences so that you know all students have had the opportunity and practiced all of the competencies that you're expecting them to have. You also need to have that one exit point that I've talked about so that there isn't different ways of graduating in different programs because otherwise, how do you know that all midwives in your country will have the same standards and competencies in quality of care? Thank you.

Now, that is very important for us because the national adaptation is important. Every midwife needs to be competent and especially our community midwives. My question is, what implementation support should midwives be seeking? One of the really important things is that we have qualified and experienced midwives supporting and guiding students in practice and that ratio is achievable.

Sometimes we have clinical preceptors in practice trying to supervise 20 or 30 students at any one time and the students need to have really high quality placements across the full range of scope of practice. So students need experience in the community shadowing and following midwives there so that they are learning and developing all of the range of skills and midwife preceptors are really key to this, having skilled clinical midwives that are able to assess and teach in practice and not just the theory components and that's quite a skill. They need to be prepared to be able to do that.

To be able to assess students and effectively provide feedback and guide them and teach them takes time and we need to make sure that we prepare midwives to be able to be clinical preceptors. Thank you very much. Duncan, the UNFPA has supported midwifery education institutional strengthening and a lot of faculty development of the curriculum.

So what practical implementation pathway does UNFPA envisage in this countries whether the ones that you have supported or others to be ready to adopt or adapt the updated sample curriculum that you have presented to us? Thank you so much, Prof. And just to break protocol a bit, I must mention at the outset that Dr. Olive Tengera here was my senior in school and being that I'm in Rwanda, I'll not be fair not to acknowledge that otherwise I may not be able to go back to Kenya in her presence. Thank you so much for that question. Indeed, when we look at the implementation pathways that UNFPA has supported the countries when it comes to midwifery education, we see that for the global sample curricula that is upcoming, there has to be strong national adaptation at the country level.

And one of the key things that we think should be happening at the country level is the establishment of the national curricular taskforce to ensure that we have these embedded within the national level. Because what we see in most countries is that midwifery education seems to oscillate between the ministries of health, ministries of education, as well as the independent regulators who are the nursing and midwifery councils. And therefore there has to be a point where we are bringing all these players together to ensure that then they are able to articulate the needs of the country and have a common understanding for us to be able to move forward with a clear curriculum.

The second aspect refers to around issues to do with the gap analysis at the country level. Countries need to identify what their needs are at the country level, particularly when it comes to the volume of midwives they need, as well as the scope of practice that they have at the country level. Just from yesterday's presentations from the UNFPA regional offices, we saw that certain regions' midwives are not allowed to perform certain procedures.

And therefore there's a need for countries to map their competencies against the global competencies for midwives so that they can then be able to tell where the global competencies exceed the national competencies, then the country has to decide whether it's going to adapt to the new or need for advocacy for them to have the framework for their competencies. And one other component is around faculty development and also the preceptor programs. When we look in the countries, this is a competency-based curriculum, and we expect that you cannot use the old techniques to deliver a new thing.

The skills require people who are also being strengthened for them to be able to deliver this, and therefore we expect that faculty will be strengthened, particularly also colleagues within the clinical areas so that they can then support the students when it comes to their skills development. And the issues around clinical sites, this is a monster in the room that continues to come, where what we see most of the time is that we have an overload of students in the clinical areas, and this clearly highlights that there needs to be a mapping for the countries. When you are establishing a clinical and midwifery institution training site, do you have the adequate sites where students will get the necessary exposure that they need? Otherwise, you have students who will visit the sites, and then by the time they are finishing their rotations, they do not have, they've not achieved the minimum caseloads required and therefore limited competencies.

And therefore, we expect that by the end of it, we expect mapping to be conducted at the national level and also at the school's level to ensure that we are having the right pathway for the students. Thank you. Thank you very much.

I think what we are hearing here is that we need to contextualize as much as this is a global curriculum, we need to think around doing the mapping and contextualizing the curriculum. Thank you very much. And just to follow up, I will now come back to Dr. Main.

How can countries strengthen harmonization of midwifery education programs from a professional competencies and regulatory? Just seeing that we have nurse midwife education, which is very integral in Africa, how do you think these countries can be supported for professional mobility in order for them to have their full competencies? Thank you, Doreen. And good morning, everyone. From the perspective of EXACON, I believe regional harmonization is essential so that we can build a competent, confident and mobile midwifery workforce across the region.

However, I believe that harmonization does not mean having identical curricula in every country. It means agreeing on common minimum standards, educational standards, core competencies as well as graduate outcomes. And at the same time, we are allowing countries to adopt programs to the national context.

Now, whether through direct entry or post-nursing pathways, every midwife must demonstrate the competencies required to provide the evidence-based practice and as well as woman-centered care. Secondly, we need stronger collaborations between national regulators, ministries of health, educational institutions, so that we can align registration requirements, competencies and as well as scope of practice. In line with EXACON, we can play an important role in facilitating this at regional level in collaboration and advocating for mutual recognition of qualifications.

And this will support professional mobility and as well as maintaining patient safety and national regulatory standards. Therefore, thirdly, we need to address retention. We cannot continue to educate midwives only to lose them because of poor working conditions, limited career opportunities and also lack of professional recognition.

We need clear career progression, specialist development, continuous professional development and importantly, midwives needs to be represented in the highest levels of health management and as well at decision-making. So what we are trying to say ultimately is our goal must go beyond graduating midwives. We must create systems that allow them to practice to their full competence, grow professionally, lead and remain within the profession.
Thank you. Fantastic, thank you. And I think, let's give her a round of applause.

What we are saying is change is difficult. So as we are navigating the change to speak about competent midwives and confident midwives, depends on what we give them, the competencies that they need to go out there. They could be confidently incompetent and we will have problems.
And I think those are the challenges we are facing a lot of times. Thank you very much. Dr. Tenge, Rwanda has already started the journey to implement the new curriculum.

What are the key lessons from Rwanda's process of developing a nationally harmonized curriculum, educate a competence that is internationally aligned. And just as you tell us, let's know how you ensure that the curriculum reform translates into effective teaching and learning and competent graduates. Over to you.

Thank you very much, Prof. Dori. And thank you to give this privilege to share the experience of Rwanda. What we know the most important lesson we learn from Rwanda is that the curriculum reform is not a document, it's a system.

And a good curriculum is not on paper changes without changing or helping faculty, clinical sites, regulatory bodies for these midwives. We have learned a lot through the process of developing. It was not even developing from a fresh because we used to teach midwives, but it was like reviewing based on ICM standard.

I can say like four key lesson we learned, but we learned a lot. First, during the process of development, we are not alone. Minister of Health, regulators, universities, midwifery, private schools, partners, clinical sites, partners, all of us we sat together.
We didn't want to handle the curriculum to schools to teach. And this helped us to have that adoption easier and validation easier. That's what we learned as the first lesson.

The second was aligning this ICM competence based curriculum with national priorities. We used ICM global standard as a common reference point. And we moved to the conversation saying, from what each current we teach to what competent midwife must be able to do.

That is what we learned as a second lesson. The third lesson we learned was to within that alignment, to align curriculum, revise it, map it with those ICM competence, but also alongside we develop curriculum for the framework. Development for the faculty, not going with only curriculum and leaving behind the faculty.

That is not yet validated because this curriculum has been worked on and published in January, 2026. And now some institution as yesterday they presented, we have 11 midwifery schools, but like four have started to implement it while phasing out the existing one and also others to adopt it. What we learned from this, it is with organized curriculum.

It is not only to organize curriculum and leaving the teacher behind as I said. We worked with a consultant firm from Gothenburg University. They are professors midwifery, used global standard of midwifery to see how we can map the needs assessment done previously before implementing, developing this curriculum to respond on those faculty needs is the way we started that development framework for faculty.
We used the Delphi study. It is still undergoing, but we had professors on different steps. Now we did like two rounds.

And from there, we validated those two rounds. We are remaining for having final document for the development framework for the faculty based on the needs they presented in different publication we will find on the website. This will help us implement this curriculum easily based on the needs of assessed from educators, also to train them for not only the existing educators, but also newly appointed educators, mentors, receptors on different domain in that framework we developed.
Is what I can say like for this only, right? Thank you. Fantastic. And what I'm taking home from here is stakeholder involvement is very important.

Sure. It is one of the red tapes and yellow tapes, but we usually say, mtaka shambunguni sharti ainame. That is Swahili, that if you want something under the table, you're gonna bend, but we have to bend even if it is backwards to get a stakeholder investment.
Thank you very much. Let's give another round of applause. Now we get to a space where we are going to have a discussion.

And the first one is about the faculty and competencies. Anything new we need to orientate people. How can African countries strengthen faculty development, clinical education, aligning educational and regulatory systems to support competency assurance and cross border mobility? And I'll start with Dr. May.

I believe strengthening midwifery education has three key actions. We need to invest in faculty development as it has been said this morning through continuous training, mentorship, and as well as updating educators' clinical skills. The second one is strengthening clinical education.

This will ensure that we have competent preceptors, adequate clinical placements, and as well as simulation-based learning so that students can demonstrate their competencies in their practice. And all this has been mentioned again this morning. Align the educational and regulatory standards so that it can ensure that comparable competencies, accreditation and professional recognition across countries.
And for sure, Exxon can support this through the regional collaboration and as well as educator development and accreditation and quality assurance. Thank you. Fantastic, thank you.

Dr. Shikoku, we were talking about the new curriculum. How do you envision the faculty development within our context? Thank you so much, Pro. Without adding to what my colleague has mentioned, I think one other additional thing I look at here is the South to South collaboration of peer to peer learning.

There's so much growth and experience within our countries. And for those who have already developed within these faculty development setups, I think it's a good opportunity for those who are upcoming to get to learn from them on what is existing. Secondly, we need to establish the regional hubs so that we are not regional hubs of excellence when it comes to midwifery education.

And this can be very good avenues to ensure that there's a pooled manpower when it comes to training of master trainers that will be key in cascading the faculty development programs to the other countries. But then for us to be able to start, there has to be key investments within these setups, particularly around the simulation learning investment. Because what we've seen from experience, we assume that students are the ones who are not doing the simulation.

But to shock you, majority of our educators also don't go through the simulation. And it was not shocking when we were having some of the assessments within the institutions that some of the educators also do not even know the simulation equipment that are used. And therefore, there has to be a start from the faculty within the institutions, as well as we look forward to going to the students.

And lastly, just around this area of faculty development, when we speak about the simulation lab, I know UNFPA has played one of the major roles, I know together with ICM as well, in ensuring that they support for their countries to get this simulation lab equipment. And we encourage their countries through some of the match funding initiatives to also come forward so that they can benefit from this simulation equipment to support faculty development. Fantastic, thank you.

And I will actually follow through with that financing because everybody here I'm sure is wondering, do I go into my pocket to implement this new project? So, Kate, if we reconvene in the next 12 to 24 months, what evidence should demonstrate progress beyond curriculum implementation? And how can it be sustained in the era of looking for finances? I think we heard yesterday around the economic investment that midwives can offer. So we need to future proof what we want midwifery education to look like for 20 years time. We've talked a lot around the time and investment that it takes to create quality midwifery education.
